docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: The arrays are saved in data/inputs.npz. The report shows a summary of what was read (number of loops and anchors, loop lengths), the figure of the anchor profiles and loop lengths, the loop matrices, the extra tracks, and, with Hi-C, the map as it was read together with its resolution and normalisation.

docs.title: What is LoopSage?
docs.text: LoopSage is a program that turns a list of chromatin loops into an ensemble of 3D genome structures. It models how the protein complex cohesin pushes DNA through itself and builds loops, and it checks the result against your data.

docs.title: The idea in one minute
docs.text:
Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is folded. A key part of the folding is loop extrusion: a ring-shaped protein complex (cohesin) lands on the chromatin fibre and slides along it, pulling in DNA and growing a loop. It stops at roadblocks, mainly CTCF proteins bound to specific DNA sites, which are called anchors of the loop.

LoopSage reproduces this process in a computer:

  1. Input. You give the loops measured in an experiment (for example ChIA-PET, HiChIP or Hi-C loops) and a genomic region.
  2. Loop extrusion model. Each cohesin is a loop-extruding factor (LEF), a pair of legs on the chromatin fibre. A Monte Carlo algorithm moves the legs at random and keeps moves that make the loops agree better with your data. After many steps it has produced many plausible loop configurations, an ensemble.
  3. 3D structures. A short molecular dynamics simulation turns every loop configuration into a 3D polymer structure.
  4. Checks. The simulated contacts are compared with the experiment (loop strength, contact decay with distance, insulation score, compartments).
  5. Report. Everything is collected in one HTML report with figures, tables and plain-language explanations.

docs.title: Words used in these notes
docs.text: Term Meaning Bead One piece of the chromatin fibre in the model, covering a fixed stretch of DNA (for example 2 kb). The region is a chain of beads. Loop A pair of beads (left leg, right leg) held together by a LEF. Anchor A bead where loops tend to start or stop, typically a CTCF site. LEF Loop-extruding factor, the model of one cohesin complex. Monte Carlo (MC) A method that explores many configurations by random moves, accepting or rejecting each move with a probability set by an energy. Energy A number that is low when the loops agree with the data and with the physics of the model. Low-energy configurations are more likely. MD Molecular dynamics, a physical simulation of the 3D polymer. PET Paired-end tag, one sequencing read pair that supports a loop. More PET counts means a more reliable loop. BEDPE A text file format with one loop per line: two genomic intervals (the two anchors) plus a score.

docs.title: What you give and what you get
docs.text:
Input

  • A loop file: .bedpe (loops), or .bed / .narrowPeak (CTCF sites).
  • A region, for example chr1:77000000-95000000.
  • Optional: CTCF orientation (inside the BEDPE file, or read from a reference genome by LoopSage), BigWig tracks, a compartment track.

Output (in one folder per run)

  • report/report.html, the full report with figures and explanations.
  • visualizations/, every figure as PNG and SVG.
  • structures/, 3D structures (.cif), an interactive 3D viewer and videos.
  • data/, the numerical results; maps are saved as .npy files in data/metadata/.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000

Then open results/chr1_77000000_95000000_1/report/report.html in a browser. Install the program first: see Installation. All options are listed in the Reference.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
If you use LoopSage, please cite:

  • Korsak, S. and Plewczynski, D. LoopSage: An energy-based Monte Carlo approach for the loop extrusion modelling of chromatin. Methods (2024).
  • Jodkowska, K., Parteka-Tojek, Z., Agarwal, A., Denkiewicz, M., Korsak, S., Chiliński, M., Banecki, K., and Plewczynski, D. Improved cohesin HiChIP protocol and bioinformatic analysis for robust detection of chromatin loops and stripes. bioRxiv (2024). doi:10.1101/2024.05.16.594268

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer.
  • A Linux, macOS or Windows (WSL) computer. A GPU is optional: it only speeds up the 3D molecular dynamics stage.
  • About 2 GB of free disk space for the packages.

docs.title: Step by step (recommended: conda)
docs.text:
openmm (the molecular dynamics engine) and pyBigWig install most reliably from conda, so the packages are installed in two parts. hic-straw, which reads .hic files for the optional --hic reference, is installed with the package; it builds from source when no wheel exists for your system and then needs a C++ compiler and libcurl.

# 1. get the code
git clone https://github.com/SFGLab/pyLoopSage.git
cd pyLoopSage

# 2. create an isolated environment
conda create -n loopsage python=3.11 -y
conda activate loopsage

# 3. packages that are best installed from conda
conda install -c conda-forge "openmm>=8.5.1" pybigwig -y

# 4. all other packages
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 5. install pyLoopSage itself (creates the `loopsage` command)
pip install -e .

Check the installation with loopsage -h. Without installing, you can also run PYTHONPATH=src python src/run.py.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text:
Run the small demo (under a minute) and open the report it writes:

PYTHONPATH=src python demo/run_demo.py quick

The demo uses a small synthetic loop file shipped with the repository. It needs no downloads.

To run the automatic tests (several minutes):

PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest

docs.title: Choosing the 3D computing platform
docs.text: The 3D stage runs on the fastest platform it finds, in this order: CUDA (NVIDIA GPU), OpenCL, then CPU with all cores. The chosen platform is always printed. To force one, use --platform CUDA, --platform OpenCL or --platform CPU.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
A Dockerfile with CUDA support is in the repository root:

docker build -t loopsage .
docker run --gpus all -it -v "$PWD":/app loopsage

Inside the container, run LoopSage as described above.

docs.title: Optional: CTCF motif search
docs.text: To let LoopSage read CTCF orientation from a reference genome (--motif-genome), you only need a genome FASTA file, for example hg38.fa. No extra package is needed; the motif table (JASPAR MA0139.1) is included. See the CLI reference.

docs.title: Building these notes
docs.text:
The documentation is written in Markdown in the markdown/ folder and built with MkDocs:

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve          # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build          # write the site to site/

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Complete lists of everything you can set when running LoopSage.

Page What it covers Command-line interface The loopsage command, its general options and every option by topic, with defaults. Config files How to write a .ini config file, and a table of every key (including the advanced ones that have no command-line option).

Both pages are generated from the same parameter list in the code, so they always agree with the program.

docs.title: Command-line interface
docs.text:
LoopSage is run with one command. Every option below can also be written in a config file; the command line always wins.

loopsage [options]

Where options are read from

From weakest to strongest: built-in defaults, then the config file (-c), then command-line options, then -s KEY=VALUE. So a config file holds your usual settings and the command line changes one thing at a time.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Minimal run: a loop file and a region
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000

# Everything from a config file, but without the 3D stage and with info messages
loopsage -c config.ini --no-run-MD -vv

# Read CTCF orientation from the genome, keep loops with at least 3 PET counts, 4 threads
loopsage -f loops.bedpe -r chr1:77000000-95000000 --motif-genome hg38.fa --min-pet 3 -t 4

# Set any config key that has no option of its own

docs.title: Config files
docs.text:
A config file keeps all the settings of a run in one place, so a run can be repeated exactly. Pass it with -c:

loopsage -c config.ini

config_example.ini in the repository root lists every key with its default and a one-line description. Copy it and change what you need.

docs.title: How to write one
docs.text:
A config file is a plain text file in the INI format: sections in square brackets, and one key = value per line.

[input]
interaction_file = /data/loops.bedpe   ; the loops to model
chrom = chr1
region_start = 77000000                ; in base pairs
region_end = 95000000

[monte_carlo]
mc_steps = 20000
method = Annealing

[molecular_dynamics]
run_md = True

Rules:

  • Sections group the keys by topic (tables below). A key must be written in its own section.
  • Comments are whole lines starting with # or ;. A comment may also follow a value on the same line, after ;.
  • Empty values (seed =) mean "not set": LoopSage then picks a sensible automatic value.
  • Booleans are written True / False (also yes / no, 1 / 0).
  • Lists are comma-separated: bw_files = a.bw, b.bw.
  • Units may follow a number (step_size = 100 fs); the unit of each key is given in the tables.
  • Only the keys you change are needed. Anything missing takes its default.
  • Every command-line option is also a config key, but not the other way round: the config file has more (advanced) keys, marked ini only below.

Check what was used

Each run saves the full list of settings it used in config_resolved.ini inside the run folder, so any run can be reproduced from its own folder.

docs.title: Theory
docs.text:
The model behind LoopSage: loop extrusion, the energy function, Monte Carlo sampling and the 3D polymer.

  • Scope: what the model should explain, and how a few rules produce the patterns of a contact map.
  • Loop extrusion: the molecular players (cohesin, CTCF, condensin), the loop extrusion model with its assumptions, TADs and contact maps, stripes and why dynamics is needed.
  • Mechanics: Hamiltonian, phase space, ensembles, the Boltzmann law, and why an energy-based model is a good approximation for a cell that is not in equilibrium.
  • MCMC: Markov chains, detailed balance, ergodicity, ergodic means, burn-in and autocorrelation.
  • Molecular dynamics: the polymer, the force field, Newton's second law and the Langevin equation.
  • Topology: knots, links and the linking number, how it is computed in 3D, and how loops are checked for linking (optional, advanced).

docs.title: Loop extrusion
docs.text: This page explains loop extrusion, the process that folds chromatin into loops. It is about the biology and the basic ideas only. The energy function and the sampling algorithm of LoopSage come in the next sections. The boxes called In LoopSage just point to the settings where each idea appears in the program.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text: A human cell has about two metres of DNA that must fit into a nucleus a few micrometres wide. The DNA is therefore folded, and the folding is not random: places that are far apart along the DNA are often brought next to each other, and this controls which genes talk to which regulatory elements. One of the main folding mechanisms is loop extrusion. Imagine a ring that is threaded onto a rope and starts to slide along it while pulling the rope through itself: a loop of rope grows on one side of the ring. In the cell the ring is a protein complex, and the rope is the chromatin fibre.

docs.title: The players
docs.text:
The chromatin fibre is the DNA together with the proteins it is wrapped around. Over distances of thousands of bases it behaves like a long flexible rope. In all figures it is the black line.

Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex that works as a molecular motor. It holds the fibre at two points, and using the energy of ATP it moves these two points apart, pulling more and more fibre through itself. We call such a motor a loop extrusion factor, or LEF. In the figures cohesin is the purple ring.

CTCF is a protein that sticks to the DNA at places with a specific sequence, the CTCF motif. The motif has a direction, like a one-way arrow written along the DNA: it can point right (red) or left (blue). CTCF acts as a boundary element: a place where cohesin tends to stop.

Condensin is a cohesin relative that works when the cell divides. It is also a ring that extrudes loops, and in the figures it is green. We meet it at the end of this page.

One chromatin loop held by cohesin. The ring encircles the two strands at the base of the loop. The loop is the piece of fibre between the two legs of the ring, at positions mi and ni (ring i). Two CTCF proteins sit at the base, one pointing right (red) and one pointing left (blue).

docs.title: The loop extrusion model
docs.text:
The loop extrusion model (Sanborn et al. 2015, Fudenberg et al. 2016) proposes that a loop is not made by two faraway places that happen to meet. Instead, a cohesin ring sits on the fibre and reels it in from both sides, so the loop keeps growing until the ring is stopped by something.

The life of one loop. 1 A ring holds a short loop. 2 Driven by ATP, its two legs move apart and the loop grows. 3 Two CTCFs that face each other stop the legs. 4 After some time the ring unloads and binds somewhere else, and the old loop is released.

docs.title: How we describe a loop
docs.text:
First we cut the studied region into small equal pieces, called beads (for example 5 000 bases each), and number them \(1, 2, \dots, N_{\mathrm{beads}}\). A bead is simply a position on the fibre, and we write \(k\) for a general bead number.

There are usually many rings on the region at once, \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) of them, and we give every ring its own index \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N_{\mathrm{lef}}\). A ring has two legs, so ring \(i\) is described by two bead numbers,

\[ (m_i,\, n_i), \qquad m_i < n_i , \]

where \(m_i\) is the position of its left leg and \(n_i\) the position of its right leg. The loop of ring \(i\) is everything between its legs, so its size in beads is

\[ \ell_i = n_i - m_i . \]

The whole system at one moment is then just the list of all pairs,

\[ \{(m_i, n_i)\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathrm{lef}}} , \]

which is \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) pairs of numbers. This short list is all that the stochastic model of the next sections has to keep track of, and a change of the system is a change of one of these numbers.

Symbol Meaning \(N_{\mathrm{beads}}\) number of beads (genomic bins) in the modelled region \(k\) index of a bead, \(k = 1,\dots,N_{\mathrm{beads}}\) \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) number of loop extrusion factors (rings) on the region \(i,\ j\) index of a ring, \(i,j = 1,\dots,N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) \(m_i,\ n_i\) left and right leg of ring \(i\) (bead numbers, \(m_i<n_i\)) \(\ell_i = n_i - m_i\) size of the loop of ring \(i\), in beads \(L(k),\ R(k)\) how strongly a CTCF site at bead \(k\) stops a left leg, respectively a right leg (introduced below)

docs.title: What a LEF does
docs.text:
The ring is always on the fibre, and its life is a short cycle.

  1. It holds a small loop. A freshly placed ring holds a very short piece of fibre, a loop of one or two beads.
  2. It extrudes. The legs slide along the fibre: the left leg moves left (\(m \to m-1\)) and the right leg moves right (\(n \to n+1\)). The loop grows. In experiments this happens at about one thousand bases per second (Davidson et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2019).
  3. It stops when a leg meets a barrier: a CTCF with the right orientation, or another ring. The other leg may still move.
  4. It unloads and rebinds. After some time the ring leaves the fibre, the loop is released, and a ring binds again somewhere else. In a living cell the number of rings on the fibre stays roughly constant, so we can think that every ring that leaves is replaced at once.

The fuel is ATP, the energy currency of the cell. Each step of the ring uses a little ATP, and without it no loops are made (Ganji et al. 2018; Davidson et al. 2019). We do not follow this chemistry in detail. We only keep its result: legs that keep moving outward.

In LoopSage

The number of rings \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) is n_lef, and the number of beads \(N_{\mathrm{beads}}\) is n_beads. A Monte Carlo step either slides the legs of one ring or lets the ring unbind and rebind at a new place, so all n_lef rings are always on the fibre. By default the new place is random; lef_track_file (cohesin ChIP-seq signal) makes some places more likely.

docs.title: What the model assumes
docs.text:
The picture above rests on a few simple assumptions.

  1. More extrusion than sinking. On average the legs move outward, so loops grow rather than shrink. In the simplest version a leg only moves outward. In a more general version a leg does a random walk with a drift, so it can also step back sometimes.
  2. Motion is one-dimensional. A leg moves only along the fibre, like a bead on a string. Three-dimensional space matters later, when the loops are folded into a 3D structure.
  3. Rings do not cross. Two cohesin rings cannot pass through each other (see below).
  4. CTCF is a one-way barrier. It only stops a leg that comes from the correct side (see below).
  5. Rings live longer at barriers. A ring that is stopped by a CTCF pair is protected from being removed, so it stays much longer than a ring that is just sliding. This is why the loops anchored at CTCF are the ones that dominate experimental data. Typically CTCF stays on DNA for minutes and cohesin for tens of minutes (Hansen et al. 2017).
  6. The data are averages. An experiment measures millions of cells at once, each with its own loops. The model therefore describes a population of possible loop arrangements, not one fixed picture.

In LoopSage

lef_rw = true means that legs do a random walk; false means that they only extrude outward. lef_speed lets different rings move at different speeds.

docs.title: How CTCF stops cohesin
docs.text:
CTCF stops cohesin in one direction only. A forward CTCF (red) stops a leg that is moving left, head-on towards the arrow tip, and a reverse CTCF (blue) stops a leg that is moving right. So the two CTCFs at the ends of a loop must face each other (this is called convergent) to stop both legs.

Four arrangements of two CTCF sites. The pale dashed arc is the loop when the ring starts; the solid arc is the final loop. a Facing each other: both legs stop. b Facing away: nothing stops. c, d Same direction: one leg stops, the other keeps going. Dots are the legs of the ring, a bar marks a stopped leg, and an arrow a leg that is still moving.

This is exactly what is seen in data: loops with CTCF at both ends are mostly convergent (Rao et al. 2014; de Wit et al. 2015; Guo et al. 2015). If the two sites point in the same direction, one leg is free and keeps extruding, which makes a line of enriched contacts called a stripe. If they face away from each other, no loop is kept.

To use this in a model we only need to say, for every bead \(k\), how strongly it stops a left leg, \(L(k)\), and how strongly it stops a right leg, \(R(k)\). Beads that are not CTCF sites have \(L(k)=R(k)=0\). The direction of each site is read from the DNA sequence of its motif.

In LoopSage

The anchors in the input BEDPE file become the profiles \(L(k)\) and \(R(k)\). If the file has orientation columns (8 and 9) they are used directly; otherwise motif_genome switches on the CTCF motif search (motif_pfm, motif_pvalue) that finds the orientation of every anchor. With data_loss_mode = 1 the barriers are given as a 2D map of loops \((m,n)\) instead of two 1D profiles.

docs.title: Loops, TADs and contact maps
docs.text:
Hi-C is an experiment that counts how often two places of the genome touch each other. The result is a contact map: a square picture in which the pixel \((i,j)\) is darker when places \(i\) and \(j\) touch more often. Loop extrusion leaves two clear marks on it.

  • Loop dots. The two ends of a stable loop are held together, so they touch more often than expected and make a dark dot, usually at the corner of a square.
  • TADs (topologically associating domains; Dixon et al. 2012, Nora et al. 2012). These are squares along the diagonal. Inside a TAD, rings keep reeling in the whole region, so every place touches every other one. Across a TAD boundary contacts are rare. A boundary is often a pair of CTCFs facing away from each other, because neither lets rings from the other side come through.

Top: the fibre with loops of cohesin (nested loops inside two TADs) and CTCFs at the domain ends. Bottom: the contact map this arrangement would give. The two squares along the diagonal are TADs, and the dots are loops.

Experiments agree with this picture: when cohesin is removed, loops and TADs disappear, and when CTCF is removed, domains lose their sharp edges (Rao et al. 2017; Nora et al. 2017). Cohesin makes the loops, and CTCF decides where they stop.

docs.title: Rings do not cross
docs.text:
The fibre passes through the ring, so two rings on the same fibre cannot pass through one another. For two different rings \(i\) and \(j\), with loops \((m_i,n_i)\) and \((m_j,n_j)\), this means that they can lie side by side or one inside the other, but they cannot be interleaved, and they cannot share a leg.

Two cohesin loops. Side by side and nested loops are allowed. Interleaved loops (the legs alternate: mi < mj < ni < nj) and loops that share a leg are not.

As a result, rings push against each other and cannot all collapse into the same loop. They form a chain of neighbouring and nested loops, and the outer legs stay pressed against the next barrier.

In LoopSage

The interleaved case can be switched on or off with cross_loop, and the strictness is set by cross_coeff.

docs.title: Condensin and mitosis
docs.text:
When a cell divides, each chromosome must become a compact rod that can be moved safely into a daughter cell. For this the cell uses condensin (two forms, I and II). Like cohesin, condensin is an ATP-driven ring that extrudes loops (Ganji et al. 2018), but with three differences.

  1. Longer loops. Condensin makes loops of roughly a hundred thousand to a few hundred thousand bases, arranged in nested arrays along the chromosome (Goloborodko et al. 2016; Gibcus et al. 2018).
  2. No CTCF stops. In mitosis CTCF and most cohesin leave the chromosome arms. The condensin loops are not anchored at fixed motifs and form a dense bottle-brush around a central axis. TADs and CTCF loops disappear from the contact map.
  3. They can pass cohesin. Single-molecule experiments show that condensin rings can pass through each other and through other ring complexes (Kim et al. 2020). A cohesin loop and a condensin loop can therefore be interleaved.

a Two cohesins cannot pass each other. b A cohesin (purple) and a condensin (green) can. c In interphase, cohesin loops end at CTCF sites. d In mitosis, condensin loops sit around a central axis and do not depend on CTCF.

In LoopSage

A second group of extruders is added with n_lef2, next to the first group n_lef. Setting between_families_penalty = false lets the two groups pass through each other, while rings of the same group still cannot.

docs.title: Stripes and the need for dynamics
docs.text:
Not every pattern of a Hi-C map is a static picture of one loop. Many maps show stripes: thin lines that start at a CTCF site on the diagonal and run along a row (and, because the map is symmetric, along a column) for tens or hundreds of kilobases. A stripe means that one locus, the stripe anchor, touches many different loci in a row, one after the other.

Loop extrusion explains this naturally, if we allow the extrusion to be one-sided (Vian et al. 2018; Barrington et al. 2019). A ring is loaded close to a CTCF site that stops one of its legs. The other leg keeps running, so the loop grows step by step: at time \(t_1\) the loop is short, at \(t_2\) it is longer, at \(t_3\) longer still, until the moving leg is stopped by the opposite CTCF or the ring falls off. At each moment the ring holds one contact, \((m_i, n_i)\) with \(m_i\) fixed and \(n_i\) growing. A Hi-C experiment averages over millions of cells and over time, so these contacts add up to a line:

A stripe is a trajectory. The left leg of a ring rests at a forward CTCF while the right leg moves (pale to dark arcs, times t1 < t2 < t3). Each time point contributes one contact on the row of the fixed anchor, and the average over many rings and times is the stripe on the contact map.

This is an important point for the rest of the documentation. A stable, two-sided loop gives a dot, and a dot can be explained by a single static picture. A stripe cannot: the contact \((m, n)\) changes while the leg moves, and the stripe is the record of this motion. The same holds for the fuzzy "flames" that start at a loop dot, for domains whose inside is enriched, and for the way the strength of a loop depends on how long rings live on the fibre. These features only make sense when we know how long a ring stays, how fast it moves and how often it is stopped.

In short, a complete explanation of a Hi-C map needs dynamics, not only the positions of the barriers. This is exactly what drove us to build LoopSage: a model in which many rings load, extrude, stall and unload on the fibre, so that the contact map is obtained as an average over a simulated trajectory, and the same trajectory can be turned into 3D structures.

In LoopSage

Every leg \(m_i\), \(n_i\) is moved by its own Monte Carlo step: it slides as a random walk or only outwards (lef_rw), with a speed set by lef_speed. A leg that sits on a CTCF site is held there, so one-sided extrusion appears by itself when only one leg is at an anchor. Stripes are never drawn by hand in the Hi-C-like map; they come from the simulated trajectory. See the config reference.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A LEF (cohesin) sits on the fibre and reels it in from both sides. Ring \(i\) is just a pair of legs \((m_i,n_i)\), its loop has size \(\ell_i=n_i-m_i\), and the whole system is the list of the \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) pairs.
  • CTCF is a one-way barrier: facing sites stop both legs and make stable loops, sites in the same direction make stripes.
  • Stripes are the record of a leg that moves while the other rests: they need dynamics, not a single snapshot.
  • TADs and loop dots in Hi-C maps are the average footprint of many rings stopped at CTCF boundaries.
  • Cohesin rings do not cross each other, but condensin, which builds the long nested loops of mitotic chromosomes, can pass through cohesin.

docs.title: Markov chain Monte Carlo
docs.text: The sum \(Z=\sum_x e^{-E(x)/T}\) over all sets of loops is far too large to compute, and so is any average over the Boltzmann distribution. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) avoids it: it produces a long random sequence of states whose frequencies approach the Boltzmann probabilities, and averages are taken along the sequence. This page explains why that works and how to tell whether it worked.

docs.title: Stochastic process and Markov chain
docs.text:
A stochastic process is a sequence of random states \(X_0,X_1,X_2,\dots\), one per time step. In general each state could depend on the whole past. A Markov chain is a process with a short memory: the next state depends only on the present one,

\[ P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t,X_{t-1},\dots,X_0)=P(X_{t+1}\mid X_t). \]

The chain is described by its transition probabilities \(P_{ij}=P(X_{t+1}=j\mid X_t=i)\). In LoopSage a state is the whole set of loops, and a step is one attempted move (slide, rebind or an epigenetic change). The past matters only through the current loops, which is what makes the chain Markov. The samples are nevertheless correlated, because consecutive states differ by one move; this is the subject of the autocorrelation section.

docs.title: Which distribution does the chain reach?
docs.text:
A stationary distribution \(\pi\) is one that does not change under a step: if \(X_t\sim\pi\) then \(X_{t+1}\sim\pi\). The initial distribution is the distribution of \(X_0\): in LoopSage, a random start with loops placed at random. We want a chain whose stationary distribution is the Boltzmann law \(\pi_i\propto e^{-E_i/T}\) and which forgets its start.

Detailed balance is a convenient way to guarantee the first part. If \(\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}\) for every pair, then \(\pi\) is stationary. The Metropolis rule does this: propose a move to \(j\) with a symmetric proposal and accept it with probability

\[ \min\!\big(1,\,\pi_j/\pi_i\big)=\min\!\big(1,\,e^{-\Delta E/T}\big),\qquad \Delta E=E_j-E_i . \]

Moves that lower the energy are always accepted, moves that raise it with a probability that falls with \(\Delta E\) and rises with \(T\). Only the difference of energies enters, so \(Z\) is never needed.

a A three-state Markov chain and its transition probabilities. b A chain started in one state approaches the target distribution (dots). c The Metropolis acceptance as a function of \(\Delta E\) for three temperatures.

docs.title: Ergodicity
docs.text:
The second part, forgetting the start, is ergodicity. A chain is ergodic if it is

  • irreducible: from every state there is a path with non-zero probability to every other state, so no region of states is cut off;
  • aperiodic: it does not return to a state only at multiples of some period \(k>1\).

For such a chain the stationary distribution is unique, and for any start \(P(X_t=i)\to\pi_i\). In LoopSage the moves can reach any arrangement of loops (a ring can unbind and load anywhere), and the chance to stay in the same state keeps the chain aperiodic, so the chain is ergodic in principle.

In principle is not in practice. A chain can be ergodic and still trapped for a very long time. At a low temperature the sampler may stay in one valley of the energy landscape because crossing the barrier needs a move the Metropolis rule almost never accepts. This is why LoopSage uses annealing: it starts hot, where barriers are easy to cross, and cools down so that the chain settles in a deep valley.

a A chain on a connected graph is irreducible; a disconnected one is not. b A chain on a double well mixes at a high temperature and is trapped at a low one. c The running mean reaches the ensemble average only for the mixing chain.

docs.title: Ergodic means
docs.text:
An ergodic mean is the average of a quantity \(x_t=f(X_t)\) along the chain,

\[ \bar x_T=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T}x_t \;\longrightarrow\; \langle x\rangle=\sum_i \pi_i f(i)\qquad (T\to\infty). \]

The right-hand side is the ensemble average, the average over the Boltzmann distribution. The theorem says that the time average along one long ergodic chain equals it. This is what makes the whole method work: we never sum over all states, we average over snapshots.

Almost everything LoopSage reports is an ergodic mean over the snapshots after the burn-in: the contact map implied by the loops, the mean loop length, the unfolded fraction, the average of each energy term, the occupancy of each bead by a loop leg, and the insulation or stripe profiles computed from the averaged map. The averaged MD contact map is the same kind of quantity over the 3D frames. These are meaningful when the chain has converged and the number of snapshots is large compared with the correlation time.

What is not an ergodic mean: a single snapshot, the last snapshot, the minimum energy found, and any average that includes the burn-in or the annealing phase (the chain is then not stationary).

docs.title: Reading a run: the burn-in
docs.text:
A chain that starts away from the typical states first drifts, and only later fluctuates around a constant level. The drifting part is the burn-in and is discarded. The mean loop length is a good indicator: at the start the rings are short, it rises, and in equilibrium it should stay almost constant with fluctuations. A curve that keeps rising or falling is not equilibrated.

Two real LoopSage chains (Metropolis, \(T=1\), 250 beads, 39 extruders, 200 000 steps, one snapshot per 40 steps). a The trace of the mean loop length. b The running mean after the burn-in. c The autocorrelation function. Purple is chain 1 and black chain 2.

docs.title: Autocorrelation: how long the chain remembers
docs.text:
Consecutive snapshots are similar, so the samples are not independent. The autocorrelation function measures how similar a quantity is to itself after a delay of \(k\) snapshots (the lag),

\[ \rho(k)=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(x_t,\,x_{t+k})}{\operatorname{var}(x_t)},\qquad \rho(0)=1 . \]

How to read it. \(\rho(k)=1\) means the two values are identical, \(\rho(k)=0\) means that they are unrelated, and a negative value means that they tend to be opposite. A plot of \(\rho\) against \(k\) starts at 1 and decays. The lag at which it reaches about 0 is the time after which the chain has forgotten where it was: samples further apart than that are practically independent. A curve that stays high for hundreds of lags says that the chain moves slowly through the states.

The decay is summarised by the integrated autocorrelation time,

\[ \tau_{\mathrm{int}}=1+2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho(k), \]

the number of snapshots that are worth one independent sample. With \(T\) snapshots the effective sample size is

\[ \mathrm{ESS}=\frac{T}{\tau_{\mathrm{int}}}, \]

and the error of an ergodic mean is about \(\sigma/\sqrt{\mathrm{ESS}}\), with \(\sigma\) the standard deviation of the quantity. In the figure above \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\approx240\) and \(740\) snapshots, so each chain of 4750 snapshots after the burn-in is worth only about 20 and 6 independent samples of the mean loop length. This is the honest measure of how much the run knows.

In practice

Plot the trace: it should fluctuate around a constant after the burn-in. Run two chains from different random starts (replicas): their running means must agree, as in panel b. Read \(\tau_{\mathrm{int}}\) off the autocorrelation: if it is a large share of the run, increase n_steps, not only the number of snapshots (saving more often adds correlated samples, not new ones). The Monte Carlo page lists the settings, and the report shows the drift of the energy between the two halves of the run.

docs.title: Mechanics of LoopSage
docs.text: LoopSage assigns an energy to every set of loops and samples sets with probability \(\propto e^{-E/T}\). This page explains where that idea comes from, why it is only an approximation for a living cell, and what is kept from the exact theory. New words are defined when they appear.

docs.title: The mechanical Hamiltonian
docs.text:
In classical mechanics a system of \(N\) particles is described by the positions \(q\) and momenta \(p\) of all particles. Together they form a point \((q,p)\) in the phase space, a space with \(6N\) coordinates (three positions and three momenta per particle). The Hamiltonian \(H(q,p)\) is the total energy as a function of this point: kinetic plus potential, for example \(H=\tfrac12p^2+\tfrac12q^2\) for an oscillator. It determines the motion through Hamilton's equations,

\[ \dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p},\qquad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}, \]

where a dot is the derivative with respect to time. The system moves along a curve of constant energy.

This needs \(H\) to be differentiable: the force is the derivative of the energy, so a smooth landscape gives a well-defined motion. The energy of the loop model is not like that. A loop has integer positions \((m,n)\) on a grid of beads, so there is no derivative, and the loops do not follow equations of motion. Loop extrusion in LoopSage is a statistical model, and for it only a weaker notion of Hamiltonian is kept.

a A mechanical state is a point in phase space and moves along a curve of constant energy. b An energy landscape turns into probabilities by the Boltzmann law; a higher temperature allows higher energies. c Ensembles differ by what is held fixed.

docs.title: The statistical Hamiltonian
docs.text:
In statistical physics the Hamiltonian can be any function \(E(x)\) that gives the energy of a state \(x\), with no need for derivatives or motion. Then the probability of a state at temperature \(T\) is the Boltzmann law,

\[ P(x)=\frac{1}{Z}\,e^{-E(x)/T},\qquad Z=\sum_x e^{-E(x)/T}. \]

\(Z\) is the partition function, the number that makes the probabilities sum to one. Low-energy states are likely, and \(T\) sets how much higher energy is tolerated. In LoopSage \(T\) is in arbitrary units, because the energy itself is made of effective terms (folding, binding, crossing) and not of physical joules. A state \(x\) is the complete set of loops \(\{(m_i,n_i)\}\), possibly with the epigenetic states of the beads.

docs.title: Ensembles
docs.text:
An ensemble is the set of all states together with their probabilities, for a given set of conditions. The three classical ones differ in what is held fixed.

Ensemble Fixed Exchanges with the outside microcanonical energy \(E\), particle number \(N\) nothing (isolated) canonical temperature \(T\), particle number \(N\) energy (a heat bath) grand canonical temperature \(T\), chemical potential \(\mu\) energy and particles

LoopSage uses the canonical ensemble: the number of extruders \(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\) is fixed, and the temperature \(T\) controls the fluctuations. This is why the Boltzmann law above is the right distribution, and why the Metropolis rule on the Monte Carlo page works. The grand canonical alternative, with extruders appearing and disappearing, is mimicked by the rebinding move, where one ring is removed and another loaded.

docs.title: A cell is not in equilibrium
docs.text:
The Boltzmann law describes a system in equilibrium. A cohesin ring is not in equilibrium: it burns ATP to extrude, and it loads and unloads in a cycle. This is a driven system.

What distinguishes equilibrium is detailed balance. Let \(\pi_i\) be the probability of state \(i\) and \(P_{ij}\) the probability to jump from \(i\) to \(j\) in one step. Detailed balance says that for every pair of states the two flows are equal,

\[ \pi_i\,P_{ij}=\pi_j\,P_{ji}. \]

Nothing circulates: a film of the system looks the same played backwards. In a driven cycle (load, extrude, release) the forward flow is much larger than the backward one, so there is a steady current and detailed balance is broken. The system is then in a steady state: the probabilities \(\pi\) do not change with time, but they are not Boltzmann probabilities.

a Detailed balance: equal flows for every pair. b A driven cycle has a net current, so it is out of equilibrium. c LoopSage takes the stationary distribution and writes it as an effective energy.

docs.title: The LoopSage approximation
docs.text:
LoopSage does not model the driving. It turns the problem around: whatever the stationary distribution \(\pi\) of the loops is, write it as

\[ \pi(x)\propto e^{-E(x)/T}. \]

The energy is then an effective energy, \(E=-T\ln\pi\) up to a constant: it is not the physical energy of the ring but a compact way of saying which loop sets are likely. The terms of \(E\) are chosen to reproduce what is observed. Long loops are favoured (folding), legs prefer CTCF sites (binding), and crossing loops are forbidden (crossing). The coefficients are fitted by the optimizer to Hi-C or to the input loops.

This is an approximation with a clear limit. Equilibrium sampling gives the right average map and the right fluctuations if the effective energy is right, but it does not give the dynamics: the sampler's steps are not real time, and currents such as the directed motion of a ring are replaced by random-walk moves. Questions about speed, residence times or the order of events need a model with real kinetics.

docs.title: How detailed balance is approximated
docs.text:
The sampler (MCMC) is built so that it satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(e^{-E/T}\) by construction: a proposed move is accepted with the Metropolis probability, which makes \(\pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_jP_{ji}\) for the target distribution. Three choices keep this approximately true in practice.

  • Symmetric proposals. Sliding by \(\pm1\) is as likely as the reverse move, so the proposal does not bias the result.
  • Rebinding as an approximation. The rebinding move (load a minimal loop anywhere) is not exactly the reverse of the extrusion, so it is a loading process rather than an exactly balanced move. With uniform loading it is close to symmetric. A loading track makes it deliberately biased towards the real loading sites.
  • Annealing. With method = Annealing the temperature changes during the run, so the chain is not stationary until the end. Only the snapshots after the burn-in, when the temperature is close to its final value, are used for statistics.

In LoopSage

The energy terms and the temperature are described in Monte Carlo. The next page explains why the sampler converges to the Boltzmann distribution and how to check that it did.

docs.title: Molecular dynamics of the polymer
docs.text: The Monte Carlo stage gives sets of loops. This page explains the physics that turns them into 3D structures: how chromatin is represented as a polymer, which forces act on it, and how Newton's second law moves it. The settings are on the Molecular Dynamics implementation page.

docs.title: Polymer representation
docs.text:
A chromatin fibre has billions of atoms, and following them all is impossible and unnecessary. We coarse-grain: a stretch of a few kilobases is replaced by one bead, and only the positions \(\mathbf r_i\) of the beads are followed. Everything finer than a bead is averaged out. The result is a bead-spring chain: neighbouring beads are connected by springs (bonds), and extra terms make the chain stiff and prevent beads from overlapping.

a The fibre is replaced by beads. b A bead-spring chain with bonds, angles and excluded volume. c The size \(R\) of a chain of \(N\) beads grows as \(N^ u\); the exponent \( u\) depends on how crowded the chain is.

The size of a chain is measured by the radius of gyration \(R\) (the typical distance of the beads from the centre). It follows a power law \(R\sim N^{ u}\) in the number of beads. An ideal chain that ignores itself has \( u=1/2\), a chain with excluded volume swells to about \( u\approx0.59\), and a compact globule has \( u=1/3\). Chromatin in the nucleus is closer to the compact end, which is why loops and attractive forces matter.

docs.title: The force field
docs.text:
A force field is the list of potential energies \(U\) of the model. The force on bead \(i\) is \(\mathbf F_i=-\nabla_i U\), the slope of the energy landscape pointing downhill. LoopSage uses these terms for chromatin.

Bonds keep neighbours at distance \(r_0\) with a harmonic spring, \(U=\tfrac12k(r-r_0)^2\). The constant \(k\) is large, so the chain is practically inextensible.

Angles give the fibre a stiffness: \(U=\tfrac12k_\theta(\theta-\pi)^2\) is lowest when three neighbouring beads lie on a straight line (\(\theta=\pi\)). A small \(k_\theta\) gives a flexible fibre, a large one a stiff rod.

Excluded volume is a repulsion at short distance. Without it the chain can pass through itself, which is not possible for a real fibre. LoopSage uses a soft power law, \(U_{\mathrm{ev}}\propto(\cdot/(r+r_s))^{p}\), whose steepness is set by \(p\). A softer wall allows strands to cross, which is related to what topoisomerases do (see Topology).

Loop springs are the link to the Monte Carlo. For every loop of the current snapshot, the two anchor beads are connected by a stiff spring with a short rest length, so they sit next to each other and the fibre between them forms a loop.

Compartment attraction (optional) is a Gaussian well \(U=-s\,e^{-r^2/2w^2}\) between beads of the same epigenetic state: same-type chromatin attracts, so A and B domains separate.

a The harmonic bond and angle potentials. b The excluded-volume wall for three exponents, and the Gaussian well of the compartments. c A loop spring between two anchors.

docs.title: Newton's second law and the Langevin equation
docs.text:
Newton's second law says that mass times acceleration equals the total force. For a bead in a viscous fluid there are two more forces besides \(-\nabla U\): a friction \(-\gamma m\dot{\mathbf r}\) that slows the bead, and random kicks \(\boldsymbol\xi(t)\) from collisions with the surrounding molecules,

\[ m\,\ddot{\mathbf r}=-\nabla U-\gamma m\,\dot{\mathbf r}+\boldsymbol\xi(t). \]

This is the Langevin equation. The friction coefficient \(\gamma\) and the strength of the kicks are tied together (the fluctuation–dissipation relation), and together they set the temperature of the system: the heat bath. The beads then sample positions with probability \(\propto e^{-U/k_BT}\), the same Boltzmann law as in the Mechanics page, now for the shape of the polymer given the loops.

a The forces on one bead. b Time is cut into steps \(\Delta t\). c The mean squared displacement grows as \(t^2\) at short times and as \(t\) at long times.

docs.title: Time stepping
docs.text: The equation cannot be solved exactly, so time is cut into small steps \(\Delta t\). In each step the forces are computed from the current positions, and velocities and positions are updated a little. After many steps the chain has moved. The step must be small compared with the fastest motion (the vibration of the stiff bonds and loop springs), otherwise the numbers grow without bound and the simulation blows up. Friction makes the dynamics overdamped at long times: the mean squared displacement of a bead grows as \(t^2\) at short times (free flight) and as \(t\) at long times (diffusion).

docs.title: Why MD after Monte Carlo
docs.text: The Monte Carlo has no geometry, it only knows which beads are tied. MD adds the missing physics: the fibre has a thickness, cannot cross itself, and has stiffness, so loops compete for space. Between two Monte Carlo snapshots the loops change little, so the chain is not restarted but relaxed from the previous structure for a number of steps with the new springs. The set of frames is the 3D ensemble, and its average is again an ergodic mean (see MCMC).

docs.title: Scope: what the model explains
docs.text: Before the details, one question: what do we want from a model of loop extrusion? This page sets the goal and the logic of the approach. The next pages explain the physics (Mechanics), the sampling (MCMC) and the 3D polymer (Molecular dynamics). For the biology of cohesin and CTCF see Loop extrusion.

docs.title: From rules to a heatmap
docs.text:
A Hi-C map is a matrix: entry \((i,j)\) counts how often two regions \(i\) and \(j\) of the genome were found close together in space. It shows patterns: squares along the diagonal, dots at their corners, lines called stripes, and a checkerboard. The model asks a generative question: which small set of rules produces these patterns, without drawing any of them by hand?

The rules of loop extrusion are few. A ring (cohesin) loads on the fibre. It extrudes a loop. CTCF can stop it. Rings do not cross each other. Because the process is random, a single moment is one random set of loops. The contact map is the average over many such sets: two regions are in contact often when many of the sets have a loop between them.

a The rules produce random loop states; their average is the contact map. b Patterns that the rules can explain. Compartments are the exception: they need an extra ingredient.

docs.title: Which patterns can occur
docs.text:
TADs (topologically associating domains) are squares along the diagonal: regions that contact each other more than their surroundings. They appear when loops grow between two boundaries and cannot leave the domain.

Loop dots are single bright points at the corner of a domain. They appear when a ring is stalled at two anchors that face each other (convergent CTCF) and stays there for a long time.

Stripes are lines starting at one anchor. They appear when one leg of the ring is held at an anchor and the other keeps extruding, so the anchor touches everything along one side.

A/B compartments are a checkerboard: active (A) and inactive (B) chromatin each prefer their own kind. Extrusion alone does not make them, and it even weakens them by mixing the regions. They need an attraction between like chromatin, which LoopSage can add with the epigenetic model and the compartment force.

docs.title: The two questions
docs.text:
The model has to answer two different questions, and it uses a different tool for each:

  1. Which sets of loops are likely? This is a question about probabilities. It is answered by an energy function and a Monte Carlo sampler (Mechanics and MCMC).
  2. What does the chromatin look like in 3D when a set of loops is present? This is a question about motion and shape. It is answered by molecular dynamics of a polymer (Molecular dynamics).

What the model is and is not

LoopSage is a statistical model of loops: it reproduces the distribution of loops and the average structure, not the movie of one cohesin ring in real time. Its parameters (\(N_{\mathrm{lef}}\), the energy coefficients, the temperature) are effective numbers, which the optimizer can fit to the data.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text: This page explains the topological side of LoopSage: whether the loops of a 3D structure are interlocked, how this is measured, and which optional switches model it. It is an advanced, optional feature. Nothing here runs by default and the default model is unchanged.

docs.title: Why look at topology?
docs.text:
A chromatin fibre is a very long thread. In the nucleus a thread cannot pass through another thread (the two strands repel each other), unless an enzyme, a topoisomerase, cuts one strand, passes the other one through and joins the cut again. Because of this rule, the way two pieces of the fibre are wound around each other is not changed by the usual motion of the chain. It is a conserved property, called its topology.

In loop extrusion this matters in a concrete way. Each ring holds a loop, and loops of different rings sit close to each other in space. Two loops can lie next to each other like two separate rubber bands, or they can pass through each other like two links of a chain. The second case is called catenation, and it can only be created or removed by strand passage.

docs.title: Knots and links
docs.text:
Topology studies shapes that can be deformed without cutting or gluing (a deformation without cutting is called an isotopy). Two objects are the same if one can be deformed into the other in this way. A coffee cup and a doughnut are the same in this sense, a doughnut and a sphere are not.

For closed threads there are two basic objects.

  • A knot is one closed curve in 3D space. The simplest closed curve is a round circle, the unknot. A knot is a closed curve that cannot be deformed into a circle without cutting it. The simplest one is the trefoil.
  • A link is a set of two or more disjoint closed curves, called its components. The simplest link is the Hopf link: two circles, each passing through the other. The unlink is the trivial case, curves that can be pulled apart.

A knot is one closed curve (here the trefoil), a link is several closed curves (here the Hopf link), and in the unlink the curves can be separated. At every crossing the strand that is cut by a gap passes under the other one.

docs.title: In which dimensions do they exist?
docs.text:
A closed curve is a one-dimensional object. Knots and links need room to go around each other, and the number of dimensions of the space decides how much room there is.

Space What happens a line (1D) a closed curve does not even fit the plane (2D) no knots and no links. Every simple closed curve (one that does not cross itself) is equivalent to a circle (the Jordan curve theorem), and two disjoint circles are either one inside the other or side by side, never interlocked ordinary space (3D) knots and links exist, and there are infinitely many different ones 4D and higher no knots and no links: there is a free direction, so any closed curve can be unknotted and any two curves can be pulled apart

Knots and links are therefore a purely three-dimensional phenomenon. This is why topology cannot be read from the contact map or from the loop list alone, and why LoopSage needs the 3D structures (the molecular dynamics stage) to study it.

docs.title: Knots or links?
docs.text:
For the loops of LoopSage the natural object is a link, for four reasons.

  1. The fibre is not closed. A chromosome piece is an open chain with two free ends, and strictly speaking an open chain cannot be knotted, because a knot needs a closed curve.
  2. Loops are closed curves. The two legs of a ring, \(m_i\) and \(n_i\), are held together by the ring, so they are neighbours in space. The stretch of fibre between them, closed by this short gap, is a closed curve (see below).
  3. The question is about pairs. Loops are short and rarely knot on their own. The biologically interesting question is whether two different loops are interlocked, that is, whether the set of loops forms a link.
  4. The ring itself is a link. A cohesin ring that holds DNA inside it is thought to be topologically linked with it (the ring entraps the fibre).

The tools that analyse knots of a single chain, such as the Python package Topoly (Dabrowski-Tumanski et al. 2021), compute polynomial invariants (Alexander, Jones, HOMFLY-PT) of a closed curve. They are the right tool to ask whether a protein or a closed DNA ring is knotted, and they can also compute linking numbers. LoopSage needs one quantity for many pairs of loops in thousands of frames, so it uses its own small implementation of the linking number, defined next. It does not depend on any external topology package.

docs.title: The linking number
docs.text:
The linking number \(\mathrm{Lk}\) is the simplest and most useful number that tells how two closed curves are interlocked. It is defined for two oriented curves (we choose a direction along each curve). Draw the pair on a plane, so that at every crossing one strand is over and the other is under. A crossing between the two curves gets a sign \(\varepsilon=\pm1\):

  • \(\varepsilon=+1\) (right-handed) if the over strand has to be rotated counter-clockwise (by less than half a turn) to point along the under strand,
  • \(\varepsilon=-1\) (left-handed) otherwise.

Then

\[ \mathrm{Lk}(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) \;=\; \frac12 \sum_{\text{crossings between } \gamma_1 \text{ and } \gamma_2} \varepsilon . \]

Crossings of a curve with itself are not counted. Every crossing between the two curves is counted once, and half of the sum is used because, as in the Hopf link, the curves pass each other in pairs.

a The sign of a crossing. b The Hopf link has two crossings of sign +1, so Lk = +1. c Two circles that overlap in the picture but are not interlocked: the same curve is over at both crossings, the signs cancel and Lk = 0. Counting crossings alone would be misleading.

The most important properties are the following.

  • \(\mathrm{Lk}\) is an integer, and it does not depend on how the curves are drawn: any deformation without cutting leaves it unchanged. It is an invariant.
  • If \(\mathrm{Lk}\neq0\) the curves are linked. The reverse is not true: there are linked curves with \(\mathrm{Lk}=0\) (the Whitehead link), so \(\mathrm{Lk}=0\) only says that the simplest test finds no linking.
  • When a strand of one curve is passed through the other curve (what a topoisomerase does), \(\mathrm{Lk}\) changes by exactly \(\pm1\).
  • Reversing the direction of one curve changes the sign of \(\mathrm{Lk}\). We therefore report \(|\mathrm{Lk}|\) and call a pair linked if \(|\mathrm{Lk}|\ge 1\).

docs.title: The same number as an integral
docs.text:
The linking number can also be written without any drawing. Let \(\mathbf r_1(s)\) and \(\mathbf r_2(t)\) be points of the two curves. Then

\[ \mathrm{Lk}(\gamma_1,\gamma_2) \;=\; \frac{1}{4\pi}\oint_{\gamma_1}\oint_{\gamma_2} \frac{(\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)\cdot(\mathrm d\mathbf r_1\times \mathrm d\mathbf r_2)}{\lVert \mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2\rVert^{3}} . \]

This is the Gauss integral (Gauss, 1833). Its meaning is geometric. The unit vector \((\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)/\lVert\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2\rVert\) that points from one curve to the other changes as the two points move along their curves, and it covers the sphere of directions a whole number of times. The factor \(1/4\pi\) is the inverse of the area of the unit sphere, so \(\mathrm{Lk}\) is exactly how many times the sphere is covered.

docs.title: Why is it hard to compute in 3D?
docs.text:
The drawing recipe needs a projection of the 3D curves onto a plane. For a computer model, which is a chain of beads joined by straight segments, this causes several problems.

  1. The picture depends on the viewing direction. From one direction the two loops cross twice, from another four times. Only the signed sum is the same.
  2. Some directions are bad. If we look along a direction in which two segments overlap, or a bead lies exactly behind another segment, the crossing is degenerate, and the over/under decision is not defined. One has to find a "generic" direction, or average over many.
  3. Structures are noisy. A molecular dynamics frame is a wiggling polymer with segments that pass very close to each other. A tiny change of the viewing direction can create or remove crossings.
  4. Closed curves are needed. The loops of a chain are open pieces of the fibre.
  5. There are many pairs and many frames. A region has tens of loops, so hundreds of pairs, in every analysed frame.

One pair of linked loops, taken from a 3D polymer, seen from three directions. The number of crossings changes (2, 4, and an almost edge-on view in which the crossings pile up), but half the sum of the signs is always +1, which was also computed with the Gauss integral. The pictures are generated from the actual 3D coordinates.

docs.title: What LoopSage does
docs.text:
LoopSage avoids projections completely and computes the Gauss integral directly on the 3D coordinates.

  1. Closing the loops. Every loop is the piece of the chain between the two legs of a ring, beads \(m_i,\dots,n_i\). The closing segment between the two anchors (the chord) turns it into a closed polygon. This is a good approximation because the ring holds the two anchors next to each other.
  2. Which pairs are tested. Only pairs of loops that are really two separate curves are tested. Nested or overlapping loops share a piece of the chain, so they are not two separate curves and are skipped, and a loop of fewer than 4 beads is too short to be counted as a curve. What remains are loops that lie side by side along the chain, which can still be interlocked in 3D.
  3. Exact formula for polygons. For two closed polygons the double integral is a finite sum over pairs of segments, one term for every segment of the first loop and every segment of the second (Klenin and Langowski 2000). Each term is the signed area on the unit sphere swept by the direction between the two segments, written with the four unit vectors that join their end points. The sum divided by \(4\pi\) is an integer up to rounding errors, and LoopSage rounds it to give \(\mathrm{Lk}\). It is exact for the polygon, needs no projection and has no degenerate directions.
  4. A cheap pre-filter. Two curves whose bounding boxes do not overlap cannot be linked, so the sum is only computed for pairs whose boxes overlap.

a A loop becomes a closed curve when its two anchors are joined by a chord. b Only pairs of loops that are separate curves are tested. Nested or overlapping loops and loops shorter than 4 beads are skipped.

docs.title: Linking in LoopSage
docs.text:
In LoopSage

The linking analysis is switched on with --knots (key detect_knots) and works on the 3D structures, so it needs the molecular dynamics stage (run_MD = True). The name knots is historical: the quantity that is computed is the linking number of pairs of loops, as explained above.

For every knots_stride-th MD frame LoopSage takes the loops \((m_i,n_i)\) of the Monte Carlo configuration that belongs to that frame, closes them, tests all admissible pairs and stores the pairs with \(|\mathrm{Lk}|\ge1\). From this it reports:

  • the number of linked pairs per frame, next to the number of pairs that were tested,
  • the lifetime of a link, which is the number of consecutive analysed frames in which the same pair stays linked, and how many links are formed and dissolved at each step,
  • the closest approach of two loops, and a link map, which shows where along the chromosome linked pairs occur,
  • 3D snapshots of linked examples, in which the two loops are thick, closed by their chords, and a gold marker shows where they meet.

docs.title: Why links appear and disappear
docs.text: If the excluded volume were perfect, strands could never cross, and the topology of the chain could not change during the molecular dynamics. Links would then only come and go because the loops themselves change, since the Monte Carlo trajectory moves the legs and the pair of loops that is analysed is not the same in every frame. The second source is the topoisomerase.

docs.title: The topoisomerase and the crossing counter
docs.text:
LoopSage offers two optional models of a topoisomerase II, both set in the [topology] section and both off by default.

  • random mode (ev_p, continuous_top). In every frame a random fraction ev_p of the beads has its excluded volume switched off, either scattered or as one continuous stretch (continuous_top). Strands can pass through these beads.
  • local mode (topo_mode = local). Short strand-passage events: at close contacts, a strand of topo_width beads loses its excluded volume for a short window topo_window of the frame, and then the volume is switched on again. The attempts occur at a rate topo_rate per frame and per 1000 beads, between strands closer than topo_radius bond lengths. With topo_keep < 1 a passage that creates a new link is undone with probability \(1-\)topo_keep, which models a topoisomerase that simplifies the topology.

a Random mode: in every frame some beads have no excluded volume (dashed), scattered or in one stretch, and a strand can pass through them. b Local mode: two strands come close, a short stretch of one loses its excluded volume for a short window, the other strand passes through, and the volume is restored. A passage that creates a new link can be undone.

The crossing counter (track_crossings, checked every track_every MD steps) detects two bonds that pass through each other between two checks. Crossings that occur with the excluded volume on are leaks of the force field, and crossings through a switched-off bead are passages.

How easily strands cross is controlled by the excluded volume \(E(r)=\big(\varepsilon^2 s/(r+r_0)\big)^{p}\), where \(s\) is the strength (ev_ff_strength), \(p\) the exponent (ev_ff_power), \(r\) the distance between two beads and \(r_0\) a small softening length. Two bonds can only cross if four bead pairs overlap, so the barrier for a crossing is the lowest value of the sum of \(E\) over these four pairs, in units of \(k_BT\). A barrier of a few \(k_BT\) is crossed easily, and about \(10\,k_BT\) or more keeps the chain intact. The topology report prints the barrier of the current setting, and ev_barrier_target is the barrier for which it suggests a new ev_ff_strength.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Key Meaning detect_knots (--knots) linking analysis of the loops in 3D knots_stride analyse every n-th MD frame topo_mode random (default) or local topoisomerase model ev_p, continuous_top random mode: share of beads without excluded volume, and whether they form one stretch topo_rate, topo_radius, topo_width, topo_window local mode: rate, reach, strand length and duration of the passage events topo_keep local mode: probability to keep a passage that creates a link (1 = no bias) track_crossings, track_every count chain crossings, and how often to check ev_barrier_target barrier (in \(k_BT\)) used to suggest ev_ff_strength

All keys are described in the config reference, and examples/11_topology_links.ini is a ready example.
